claims.text: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure composed of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
Dislocation accumulation at lamellar phase interfaces limits room-temperature ductility and promotes brittleness.
High-pressure, high-temperature treatment in a hexahedron-anvil apparatus will cause partial recrystallization.
High-pressure, high-temperature treatment will homogenize the alloy microstructure.
The treatment will produce a refined microstructure.
The treatment will make sharp lamellar phase boundaries blurred or more gradual.
High pressure suppresses crack growth during treatment.
High temperature promotes dynamic recrystallization at and near lamellar interfaces.
More gradual phase boundaries diminish dislocation pile-ups during deformation.
Diminishing dislocation pile-ups reduces local stress concentrations during deformation.
Reducing local stress concentrations improves room-temperature tensile ductility.
The treated alloy will have greater room-temperature elongation to failure than the untreated alloy.
The treatment will maintain or slightly increase yield strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The treatment will maintain or slightly increase ultimate tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The proposed processing window uses pressures of several GPa and temperatures near the alloy's recrystallization range, followed by controlled cooling.
The expected benefit may not persist outside the proposed pressure and temperature window or in alloys with substantially different microstructures.
Failure to achieve at least a 20% statistically significant increase in elongation while maintaining or increasing tensile strength would falsify the hypothesis.
